issues.legal_issue: Property acquired in the names of a family manager and a member who managed family assets belonged to the family estate rather than being their separate property.
material_facts: The dispute concerned whether an acquired property belonged to a family governed by Marumakkathayam law or was the separate property of two family members.
The female family manager and her son, who managed family properties on her behalf, were named in transactions connected with the acquisition.
The family had income-producing properties from which the disputed property could have been purchased.
The son managed family properties and had access to their income and accounts, but withheld the family and personal accounts and did not prove that he had personal funds to pay for the acquisition.
The female manager’s strong claim to exclusive title was not supported by evidence sufficient to rebut the presumption arising from her position as manager.
issues.conclusion: The property belonged to the family estate, and the appeal challenging that finding was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Marumakkathayam law, a property acquired in the name of a karnavan or karnavati carries a strong, rebuttable presumption that it is tarwad or tavazhi property. There is no presumption either way for property acquired in the name of a junior member; that question is decided on the facts. A person who actually manages family property and stands in a fiduciary relationship with its members may have the circumstances of that management considered when deciding ownership, and those circumstances may shift the burden of proving separate title. The Court relied on Govinda v. Nani, (1913) 36 Mad. 304; Dharnu Shetty v. Dejamma, A.I.R. 1918 Mad. 1367; Soopiadath Ahmad v. Mammad Kunhi, A.I.R. 1926 Mad. 643; Thatha Amma v. Thankappa, A.I.R. 1947 Mad. 137; and Chathu Nambiar v. Sekharan Nambiar, A.I.R. 1925 Mad. 430. It distinguished the Hindu joint-family presumption based on proof of a sufficient family nucleus from the rule applicable to acquisitions by a junior member of a tarwad.

rule.if: marumakkathayam_family_property_dispute and property_acquired_in_legal_manager_name and family_had_income_sufficient_to_fund_acquisition and family_member_managed_family_assets and family_member_had_access_to_family_accounts and relevant_accounts_were_withheld and personal_funding_was_not_proved

predicates.marumakkathayam_family_property_dispute: The parties disputed whether an acquired property belonged to a family governed by Marumakkathayam law.
predicates.property_acquired_in_legal_manager_name: The property was acquired in the name of the family’s legal manager.
predicates.family_had_income_sufficient_to_fund_acq: The family owned income-producing property capable of providing funds for the acquisition.
predicates.family_member_managed_family_assets: A family member who was not the legal manager actually managed the family’s properties.
predicates.family_member_had_access_to_family_accou: The family member who managed the properties had access to their income and accounts.
predicates.relevant_accounts_were_withheld: The family member who managed the properties withheld the family and personal accounts relevant to the acquisition.
predicates.personal_funding_was_not_proved: The family member who managed the properties did not prove that personal funds paid for the acquisition.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns family-property ownership and the stated acquisition, management, funding, and account facts are present, the rule’s output is that the property is family property.
